decisions.label: Partner with an institution
decisions.framing: A collector does not have to found a new institution to keep a collection together and publicly accessible. It can be placed with one that already exists.
relevantWhen: They want the collection to stay publicly accessible.
They do not want to build and operate a museum.
An existing institution is a natural fit for what the collection contains.
They are willing to give up some ownership or some control.
They want institutional infrastructure for conservation, exhibitions, and public access.

values: A dedicated building at the university
University holds and shows the collection (both founders deceased)
None; galleries within the museum's own expansion
Governed by the documented loan terms
Loans to 550+ institutions; own free museum
The foundation, and later its own museum

questions: Does the collection have to remain together?
How long does the arrangement last?
Who pays for conservation, insurance, and installation?
How much control does the collector retain?
What happens after the collector dies?
Can either party end the arrangement?
sources: SFMOMA; the Doris and Donald Fisher Collection

topics.title: The Great Wealth Transfer and Art
topics.intro: Over the coming decades an unprecedented amount of private wealth will pass between generations. A large share of it is held by people who also own art, which puts the question of what becomes of a collection at the center of a much larger transition.

facts.label: Projected global wealth transfer over the coming decade (order of magnitude; sources and window vary)
Illustrative art-and-collectibles exposure implied under a modeled UHNW-share assumption — a Deloitte model, not a reported count
Share of inherited art that is retained rather than sold — the transition is usually about a change of hands, not a sale

sections.heading: The scale of the transition
sections.body: The wealth passing to heirs over the next decade is measured in tens of trillions of dollars, and a meaningful portion of it sits in art and collectibles. The headline figures are modeled estimates, not counts, and should be read as orders of magnitude.

sections.heading: Why ownership transition matters even without a sale
sections.body: Most inherited art is kept, not sold. That means the central event for a collection is usually a change of custody and responsibility, not a moment in the market, and it is exactly the moment that is most often unmanaged.

sections.heading: What it means for collections
sections.body: As collections change hands at scale, more families face the same set of decisions at once, with limited guidance on how others have handled them. That is the territory the Collection Index maps.

sources: Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting

topics.title: Estate Planning and Art Collections
topics.intro: Art does not move through an estate the way financial assets do. It is illiquid, taxed differently, expensive to hold, hard to divide, and often wanted by some heirs and not others. This is how that landscape works, and where it turns on professional advice.

facts.label: Federal estate & gift tax exemption per individual (2026)
Maximum federal rate on long-term gains from collectibles, vs 20% on most other assets, plus the 3.8% net investment income tax where it applies
Basis is generally stepped up to fair market value at death (IRC §1014)

sections.heading: What makes art different
sections.body: Illiquidity (a work cannot be partially sold to pay a tax bill), a higher collectibles capital-gains rate, estate-tax exposure at full value on an asset that produces no income, qualified-appraisal requirements, the cost of physical custody, and the problem that a single work cannot be divided among several heirs.

sections.heading: The decisions this forces
sections.body: Keep or sell; who receives the works; keep the collection intact or divide it; gift during life or transfer at death; give to charity and in what form; use a foundation or a trust.

sections.heading: The federal tax framework
sections.body: The 2026 federal estate and gift tax exemption is about $15M per individual with a 40% top rate; long-term gains on collectibles are taxed at a 28% federal maximum plus the 3.8% NIIT where applicable; and basis is generally stepped up to fair market value at death. Every figure here must be verified against the primary source before it is relied upon.

sections.heading: Charitable gifts of art
sections.body: A donor can generally deduct fair market value for a long-term-held work given to a public charity only if the charity's use is related to its exempt purpose (the related-use rule); deductions are capped as a share of adjusted gross income; and non-cash gifts above $5,000 require a qualified appraisal and IRS Form 8283, with high-value art reviewable by the IRS Art Advisory Panel.

sections.heading: State and other jurisdictions
sections.body: State estate and inheritance taxes vary by domicile and where works are held; a handful of states levy their own with far lower exemptions than the federal one, and other countries differ more sharply still. Specific jurisdiction pages will be added only where there is enough verified material to be useful.

sections.heading: Questions to work through
sections.body: Who legally owns the collection, and through what entity? What is the current cost basis? When was each work last appraised? Do the heirs want the collection? Would a museum accept it, and on what terms? Is the estate above or below the exemption? Gift during life or transfer at death?

sections.heading: Professional roles
sections.body: A qualified appraiser establishes value; an estate and tax attorney structures the transfer and models consequences; an accountant handles filings; an insurance specialist covers valuation, transport, and storage; an art adviser or collection manager assists with records, transactions, and institutional relationships.

sources: IRS, charitable contributions of property; Form 8283; Art Advisory Panel
